claim: Breaking a Tuition Grant bond makes the student and both sureties liable for liquidated damages on the outstanding bond period; withdrawing from the course makes them liable for the grant received plus 10% compounded interest a year. Only full-time employment after graduation counts towards the bond, deferment for postgraduate study must be approved at least eight weeks in advance, and obtaining Singapore citizenship releases the student from the three-year obligation.
excerpt: B2. […] If I have […] decided to break the bond […] You will be required to pay liquidated damages for your outstanding bond period. […] B5. What happens if I am not able to find employment after graduation? A job seeker typically takes about 6 months to find a job in Singapore. […] B6. Can I fulfil my bond before I graduate (i.e. internships or working part-time during my studies)? Please note that only full-time employment after graduation will be considered towards serving your Tuition Grant bond obligation. […] B9. […] You must apply for bond deferment to pursue further studies. Please note that approval must be obtained at least 8 weeks before the start of the post-graduate studies. […] C2. […] If you have obtained Singapore Citizenship, you will be released from the 3-year bond obligation. […] D6. What happens if I withdraw from my course midway during my studies? You and your sureties will be liable to pay liquidated damages (LD) for the Tuition Grant received, computed based on the amount of grant you received, plus 10% compounded interest per annum. Late payment interest charged will apply.
interpretation: Three things here are not in any summary of the Tuition Grant and all three change the decision. First, the exposure is not limited to breaking the bond after graduating: withdrawing from the course part-way — illness, homesickness, a change of mind in second year — triggers liquidated damages on everything received, with 10% compounded interest. Second, the liability is joint, and it falls on two named sureties who are usually the student's parents, so this is a commitment the family signs, not just the student. Third, MOE's own answer to what happens if you cannot find work is that a job search typically takes about six months — which means the three years does not begin on graduation day and the clock a student is planning against is longer than three years. Nothing here says the grant is a bad deal; it says it is a contract, and it should be read as one.

claim: A Tuition Grant Agreement requires two sureties of any nationality, aged over 21 and under 65, who are not undischarged bankrupts, are not themselves Tuition Grant or Service Obligation applicants or recipients with an outstanding obligation, and are not surety to another recipient who failed to fulfil theirs.
excerpt: Criteria for sureties: Must be above 21 and below 65 years of age · Must not be an undischarged bankrupt · Can be of any nationality · Must not be a TG/ SO applicant or recipient with outstanding obligation · Must not be a surety of another TG/ SO recipient who failed to fulfil their obligation. You are encouraged to get your immediate family members to be your sureties.
interpretation: The sureties requirement is the part of the Tuition Grant that most often surprises a European family, and it is what makes the bond a household decision rather than a student one. MOE's freshmen briefing puts it plainly elsewhere: the surety must have the financial ability to assume the liability if the student fails to fulfil the bond. Two points of practical relief: sureties may be of any nationality and need not be physically in Singapore, because the agreement is signed digitally. One point of exposure: a parent under 65 today may be over 65 by the time a younger sibling applies.

claim: International students obtain the MOE Tuition Grant by electing it on the online admission application form, then decide whether to accept their place with or without it, then register and sign the Tuition Grant Agreement with two sureties after term has started — and by signing are contractually obliged to work in a Singapore entity for three years upon graduation. The grant covers only the normal duration of the programme.
excerpt: SPR and International students who are interested in obtaining the MOE Tuition Grant […] are required to indicate that they are opting for TG in their online admission application form. If they are offered a Tuition Grant together with their university place, they will need to indicate their decision if they are accepting the offer with or without Tuition Grant by 17 July 2026. […] For all non-Singaporean students (including Singapore Permanent Residents), in exchange for the grant received under the Tuition Grant Scheme, they are required to sign the Tuition Grant Agreement in which they will be contractually obliged to work in a Singapore entity for three (3) years upon graduation. […] TWO sureties of any nationality are required. […] Online Signing on TG&S Portal 19 September 2026 - 18 October 2026 […] For students who do not apply for a Tuition Grant or do not complete the registration and signing process, they will be required to pay the non-subsidised fees. […] eligible for Tuition Grant and GST subsidy from MOE up to the normal duration taken to complete a degree programme.
interpretation: The sequence is what matters and it is easy to miss: the commitment is chosen on the application form, months before anyone explains it, confirmed at offer stage in mid-July, and only signed in September or October once the student is already in Singapore with a Student's Pass and a Singpass. By the time the contract is in front of them they have flown, paid a deposit and moved in. A Danish family should treat the tick-box on the application form as the decision point, not the signature. Note also the ceiling: the grant runs for the normal duration only, so a repeated year or a change of course is paid for at the unsubsidised rate.

interpretation: Two structural facts, beyond the dates. claim: Offers from Singapore's autonomous universities are accepted through a single shared Joint Acceptance Portal by a joint acceptance deadline, rather than to each university separately.
excerpt: NUS: "Accept the offer of admission through the Joint Acceptance Portal (JAP). Acceptance indicated through the JAP will be reflected on Applicant Portal, three calendar days after the acceptance deadline." SIT: "Successful applicants who are accepting our offer may do so via the Joint Acceptance Portal by the joint acceptance deadline."
interpretation: Singapore is often described as having no central admissions system, and for applying that is true — six universities, six forms, six fees, six deadlines. It is not true for accepting. Every offer a student holds across the autonomous universities lands in one portal and is settled in one exercise against one deadline, which is closer to the Danish or Dutch model than to the American one, and which means the choice between them is made once rather than offer by offer. Nobody tells international applicants this, and it changes how the spring is planned.

interpretation: Two corrections and one gap. LASALLE's degrees were validated by Goldsmiths, University of London; they are now awarded by UAS, and a record still saying Goldsmiths is describing a qualification a 2027 entrant will not receive. The gap is more consequential: UAS names Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents as eligible for the Tuition Grant and says nothing at all about international students, and directs the question back to LASALLE and NAFA. Whether a Danish student at LASALLE can obtain the grant — and whether they would therefore be bonded — is not established here, and must not be assumed either way from what the autonomous universities do.
